title: Impossible Places: The Most Insane Houses Built in Impossible Locations
fullText: A house is supposed to be the one place on Earth that makes sense. Four walls, a roof over your head, solid ground beneath your feet. It is the one thing our species agreed on before we agreed on almost anything else. But some people looked at the most impossible spot they could find, a cliff face with a 200 m drop, a frozen wasteland where the earth never thaws, a bare rock sitting in the middle of a flooding river, and decided that was exactly where they wanted to live. A man who spent more than 20 years alone on top of a stone pillar, hauling his food up by rope, refusing to come down. A town that goes to sleep every single night underneath a slab of rock the size of a stadium. An entire community that dug down into the desert because the surface would kill them. And one small white house standing completely alone on an island so strange that the internet invented a billionaire just to explain it. These are the most insane houses ever built in the most impossible locations on Earth. Before we begin, do something for me. Drop a comment and tell us where you are watching from and what time it is right now. We want to see how far this video travels tonight. Let's start. Number 15, the tea house that was built too high on purpose. In the hills above Nagano, Japan, there is a tiny wooden hut that looks like it fell out of the sky and got caught by two trees on the way down, which is not far from what actually happened. An architect named Tedunobu Fujimori went into the mountains near his childhood home, cut down two chestnut trunks, dragged them out, and planted them upright in the ground. Then he balanced a one room tea house on top of them about 6 m in the air. No foundation in the usual sense, no supports on the sides, two rough trunks and a box. You reach it by climbing a thin ladder that leans against the trunks. There is no handrail. When you get to the top, the entrance is deliberately small. So small that you have to fold yourself forward and crawl in on your hands and knees, the way guests have entered traditional tea rooms for centuries. Inside there is barely space for two people, a small hearth and a window that frames the valley. And when the wind comes through those hills, the whole structure moves, not violently, just enough that you feel the floor shift under you and remember that there is nothing beneath you but air and two tree trunks. Fujimorei is not an amateur. He is a respected architectural historian who taught at the University of Tokyo before he ever built anything himself. He knows exactly how much height a tea house needs, which is none at all. Traditional Japanese tea houses sit low and grounded, deliberately humble, close to the earth. So, he named this one Takasugian. The name translates to something close to a tea house built too high. He has said openly that he made it taller than it needed to be and that he wanted to be able to see his hometown from up there, which is a very calm way of describing what he actually did. He climbed 6 m into the air, pulled himself through a hole barely big enough for a person, and sat down alone above a valley he had known his entire life. That urge to get above the ground. It takes us straight to a place where somebody turned it into an entire life. Number 14, the pillar in the sky. In central Georgia, in a green valley near the village of Katsky, a natural limestone tower rises straight up out of the ground. 40 m of sheer vertical rock. Sides too smooth to grip with nothing on top of it but open sky. It is called the Katsky pillar and for most of recorded history nobody could tell you what was up there because nobody had managed to get up there to look. Locals had stories about it. Some said it was a place where the old gods had been worshiped before Christianity came to Georgia. Others said something had been left up there deliberately and hidden. But the stories stayed stories because 40 meters of blank vertical rock does not care about your curiosity. Then in 1944, a team including the writer and mountaineer Alexander Jeeper finally made the climb. And what they found on top did not clear anything up. It made it worse. There were ruins. The remains of a small church built from stone. A crypt containing human bones. a wine seller carved into the rock. Someone had gone up there centuries earlier carrying building stone and mortar and wine vessels and constructed a working monastery on the summit of a pillar with no path, no stairs, and no route of any kind. Then they had left or died, and whatever they knew went with them. The pillar had held on to that for 600 years and gave up nothing else. But the story does not stop in 1944. In the 1990s, a Georgian monk named Maxim Kaftar looked at that summit and decided it was home. He had a difficult past behind him, including time in prison. He climbed the pillar and he stayed for more than 20 years. Maxim lived up there alone. In a small cell exposed to the wind and the winter, sleeping meters from a drop that would end him instantly. His food and supplies came up in a bucket on a winch, hauled hand overhand by people at the base. He used an iron ladder bolted to the rock, a climb of around 20 minutes, which he made perhaps twice a week when the weather allowed it. When journalists eventually made that climb to interview him, they asked the obvious question, "Why up here?" He told them the silence was different at the top, that down below, the noise of the world got between him and prayer, and up on the pillar, it did not. It is a beautiful answer. It is also an answer to a much easier question than the one the pillar is really asking. Because Maxim had an iron ladder, a winch, a rope, and people at the bottom sending up his bread. The men who built that church six centuries before him had none of it. And there is still no accepted explanation for how a single block of stone reached that summit. From a house you can barely reach, we go to houses where reaching them was never the hard part. Staying on them was. Number 13. The houses that lean over the edge. In the Spanish city of Quanka, in the region of Castillia Lancha, a row of medieval houses sits along the rim of a deep gorge. That part is not unusual. Plenty of old European towns cling to cliff edges. What is unusual is that these houses did not stop at the edge. They kept going. Wooden balconies push straight out past the rock and hang in open air, suspended above the drop into the Quar River below. Three stories of them stacked on top of each other, jutting into nothing. They are called the Casas Kolgadas, the hanging houses, and they have been holding on to that cliff since at least the 1400s. Most of them are gone. Erosion, fire, collapse, and simple abandonment took them over the centuries. Only a small cluster survives, restored in the 1920s, and one of them now holds a museum of abstract art. Visitors walk out onto those old wooden balconies, look down through the gaps between the boards, and feel the drop arrive in their stomach before their brain has caught up. Here is the part that stays with me. There was solid ground behind them. There was room to build backwards safely, sensibly, the way every other town in Spain did. They built out over the void anyway. Not because they had to, because from out there, hanging three floors above a gorge, you can see the entire valley and everybody in that valley can see you. If leaning out over a cliff sounds bold, wait until you meet the town that lets the cliff lean over them. Number 12, the town that sleeps under a rock. In Andalucia in the south of Spain, there is a town called Settanil de lasodeas. Walk down one of its main streets, Caye Quas del Soul, and something feels wrong before you can name it. The light is off. The street is darker than it has any right to be at midday. Then you look up. The ceiling above your head is not a building. It is not a bridge. It is a single enormous slab of basaltt. Hundreds of tons of rock hanging directly over the road, over the cafe tables, over the front doors of people's homes. The town did not build a roof. It moved in underneath one that was already there. Families have lived in that shadow for centuries. Their kitchens, their bedrooms, their cellars are tucked into the gap where the rock meets the ground. The name of the town refers to the bodeas, the wine sellers that thrived in those cool stone spaces. Some houses here are barely houses at all. They have a front wall, a door, and windows. Everything behind that is mountain. Standing under it, instinct is immediate and loud. This cannot possibly be safe. It never has come down. The overhang was carved out by the Tjo River over a stretch of time that makes the town look like it arrived yesterday. And it has hung exactly like that for as long as any record exists. Locals will tell you it is the safest street in Setanil because it never rains on Cayvas del Soul. They are not being brave when they say that. They are being accurate. That rock has already outlasted every single person who ever stood underneath it and worried. Now, from a rock heavy enough to flatten a street to a house so thin you might not call it a house at all. Number 11, the house that is barely there. In Warsaw, Poland, there is a gap between two buildings on Quadna Street. For decades, everybody walked past it. It was the kind of dead space every city has, too narrow to be anything, filling up with weeds and rubbish. An architect named Yakob Chestn looked into that gap and saw a home. The Caret House was wedged into it in 2012. At its widest point, it measures about 152 cm across. At its narrowest, 92 cm. That is less than a meter. That is narrower than most doorways you have walked through today. Inside there is a bed, a very small kitchen, a bathroom, and a workspace. You move between levels by climbing a ladder because stairs would eat the entire floor. There is no room to walk past another person. Everything folds, stacks, or disappears into the wall. The first person to live there was the Israeli writer Edgar Caret, whose family had roots in Poland and whose name the house still carries. And here is the argument that has followed it since the day it was finished. It is so narrow that under Polish building regulations, it could not be registered as a residential building. It failed the minimum width requirements outright. So, it was registered as something else. Officially, on paper, the Caret House is an art installation. So, which is it? A house the law refuses to acknowledge or a sculpture that a writer happened to sleep inside for months at a time? I have an opinion, and I suspect plenty of you are going to disagree with me. Tell me in the comments where you would draw that line. From the narrowest home in the world, we go up, a long way up to buildings that were never meant to be reached by anyone at all. Number 10, the monasteries in the clouds. In Thessal Greece, giant pillars of stone rise out of a flat plane like the fingers of something buried underneath it, hundreds of meters tall, smooth, sheer, completely hostile to anything with hands and feet. and on top of them impossibly sit monasteries. The place is called Meteora from a Greek word meaning suspended in the air. The monks came here from around the 14th century. First as hermits living in caves at the base, then climbing higher and higher. They were escaping two things at once. The distraction of the world and the armies moving through the region. Height was not a view. Height was survival. Which leaves the question that has never gone away. If the rock is that steep, how do you build up there? The answer is somehow worse than the question. They used long ladders lashed together in sections which could be hauled up behind them the moment anyone unwelcome appeared below. Everything else, the timber, the stone, the food, the water, and eventually the people themselves went up in nets and baskets on ropes turned by a hand operated windless. Sit with that for a second. A visitor would climb into a rope net, curl up, and be lifted straight up a vertical cliff face by monks cranking a wooden winch, swinging in open air hundreds of meters above the plane, entirely dependent on rope that somebody had made by hand. There is an exchange that travelers have been repeating since at least the 1800s. A visitor halfway up in the net asks how often they replace the rope, and the answer comes back perfectly calm when the Lord lets it break. Historians still argue about whether anyone ever really said that or whether it grew in the retelling. What is not in dispute is that the ropes and the windless stayed in use for centuries. Proper stairs were only cut into the rock in the 1920s. Six of the monasteries are still active today. The monks of Meteora built their homes above the world. Our next stop did the exact opposite. It built its homes inside it. Number nine, the village inside the volcano. In East Azerbaijan province in the northwest of Iran at the foot of an extinct volcano called Sahand, there is a village where the houses are not houses. They are cones. Tall, pale, wind-carved spikes of hardened volcanic ash. Some more than 10 m high, standing in clusters across the hillside like a stone forest. And every one of them has been hollowed out from the inside. The village is called Kandovan and people have lived inside these formations for roughly 700 years. Walk through it and the details arrive one after another. Doors set into the stone, windows cut through walls a meter thick, chimneys poking out of the very tips of the cones with smoke coming out of them right now. Laundry strung between shapes that look like they belong on another planet. Livestock in the lower chambers. Families living above them. The rock does something remarkable. It is porous and thick, which means it holds temperature. The homes stay cool through a punishing summer and hold their heat through a mountain winter with no central heating and no air conditioning anywhere in the village. The people who first cut into those cones did not know the physics of thermal mass. They knew the rock felt right. What gets me about Condon is what it is not. It is not a ruin. It is not a preserved site with a ticket booth and a rope keeping you back. It is a working village. Children walk out of those stone cones to go to school. Somebody is cooking dinner tonight in a room an ancestor carved by hand seven centuries ago in a place that looks like it should have been abandoned before it was ever finished. Some people carve into rock to survive the cold. Our next town went the other way entirely. It dug down to escape the heat. Number eight, the town that lives underground. In the middle of the South Australian desert, hundreds of kilometers from anything, there is a town where at first glance almost nobody appears to live. The streets are quiet. The landscape is bare orange dirt and low mounds. Then the details start arriving. Doors set into hillsides. Ventilation shafts rising straight out of open ground. Signs pointing to a church and a hotel that are nowhere in sight. The town is called Coober Pey and most of it is underneath your feet. It exists because of opal. In 1915, a teenage boy named Willie Hutcherson out with a prospecting party looking for gold found opal here instead. Miners came and then the desert made its position clear. Summer temperatures climbed past 40° C. And in that era with no air conditioning and no shade for a 100 kilometers in any direction, the heat was not uncomfortable. It was a threat. So the miners stopped walking home in the evening and started sleeping in their shafts. Over decades, those shafts became something else. Real homes cut back into the sandstone with bedrooms and hallways and living rooms carved first by hand and later by tunneling machines. Down there, the temperature holds at around 23° C every day all year. No heating, no cooling, no seasons at all. There are underground churches in Kubi now carved with real care into the rock and hotels where visitors sleep below the surface. The name is thought to come from an Aboriginal phrase often rendered as Koopa Piti, usually translated as something close to white man in a hole. The people who live there will tell you that is about right and they seem entirely at peace with it. Now, if you are finding these as hard to believe as I am, do me one small favor before we go any further. Hit the like button. It genuinely tells the algorithm to push this video to more people who love places like these. That is all it takes because the last seven homes on this list are where the word impossible stops being a figure of speech. Number seven, the houses at the bottom of the cold. In the Saka Republic in the far east of Russia, two settlements trade the same brutal title back and forth between them. Oyakon and Veroansk. They are the coldest permanently inhabited places on the planet where measured temperatures have fallen to around -67° C. Forget the weather for a second and ask the only question that actually matters here. How does a house even work? Start with the ground because the ground is the problem. It is permafrost. It does not thaw in summer. It is not thawed in a very long time and it is not going to thaw for you. That single fact removes the foundation of a normal house immediately. A heated building sitting flat on frozen earth slowly melts the ground beneath itself and then sinks into the mud it just made. So, the houses here go up on piles driven deep into the frozen layer, holding the entire structure off the earth with cold air moving underneath it. Then, take out the plumbing. Buried pipes freeze solid and split open, so water does not arrive the way it arrives in your home. It is delivered or collected or cut from ice and carried in. And when somebody dies, the ground refuses them, too. Families light fires over the burial site, wait, dig out whatever has softened, then light another fire. Opening a single grave can take days. Now, I already know some of you are typing that extreme cold is not the same thing as an impossible location. That there is nothing structurally impossible about a wooden house on flat ground. Fair enough. But when the earth will not hold your foundation, will not take your pipes, and will not open for your dead, I would say the ground is the impossible part. That was a place that had to lift its houses off the earth. Our next one was cut off from the earth completely until the people trapped there refused to accept it. Number six, the village that carved its own escape. High in the Thaihong Mountains in Hanan Province, China, on top of a sheer cliff, sits a village called Guolang. For generations, its people were cut off from the world below in the most literal way possible. The only route in or out was a narrow stairway carved into the rock face known as the sky ladder. Around 720 steps in places barely wide enough for one person with a drop on one side and nothing to hold on the other. The ladder was not an inconvenience. It decided things. Anyone who fell seriously ill had to be carried down it. Anyone who needed help had to hope help was willing to come up it. Villagers have described losing people simply because the mountain was in the way. They petitioned the local government for a road. The answer came back that it could not be done. The cliff was too steep, the rock too hard, the village too small to justify the cost. It was impossible. So in 1972, 13 villagers picked up hammers and steel chisels and started cutting a tunnel through the mountain themselves. No machinery, no engineers, no blasting equipment worth the name. They sold livestock and possessions to buy tools. And they hammered into solid rock in shifts day after day for 5 years, hauling the debris out by basket. They went through hammers and chisels faster than they could afford to replace them. Villagers died during the work. In 1977, they broke through. The tunnel runs more than a kilometer through the heart of the cliff, roughly 5 m high and 4 meters wide, wide enough for a vehicle. You can drive through it today. And along one side, there are more than 30 windows cut into the rock wall, opening straight out onto the drop, letting light and air into the tunnel. Every one of those openings was chipped out by hand by somebody who had been told their home was impossible to reach and decided that was not an acceptable answer. Guyong is a tourist destination now. Painters come, film crews come, and the road they all arrive on was made by 13 farmers with hand tools. From a village that fought a mountain to a house that fought for every last inch of ground it could get. Number five, the house that ate its own island. In the St. Lawrence River, in the stretch known as the Thousand Islands along the border between the United States and Canada, there is an island so small that calling it an island feels generous. It is roughly the size of a tennis court and sitting on it covering very nearly every square in of solid ground it has is a single house. It is called just room enough island and the name is not exaggerating. There is the house. There is one small tree. There is a narrow strip of ground where a person can sit and put their feet in the water. Then the river begins on all sides immediately. The family that bought it in the 1950s, the Sizelands, reportedly wanted a private retreat, somewhere quiet, somewhere nobody would find them. There is a local rule of thumb in the Thousand Islands about what counts as an island at all, involving staying above water year round and supporting at least one living tree. And this scrap of rock just barely qualified. It did not work out the way they planned, not even slightly. The house was so absurd, so perfectly ridiculous in its proportions that boats started slowing down as they passed. Then tour operators began routing past it deliberately. Then the cameras came out. Today, it is one of the most photographed spots on the entire river, and the image goes around the internet several times a year. A family went looking for a place where nobody would ever look at them. And by building on the smallest piece of land they could find, they created the one house on that river that nobody can ignore. That was a home built out of a wish to be left alone. Our next one was built out of something much harder to name. Number four, the wooden tower one man could not stop building. In the Russian city of Arcangulsk in the early 1990s, a businessman named Nikolai Sutiagen started building himself a house. He had money at the time from construction work and a difficult history behind him that included a prison sentence. The plan, as he described it, was ordinary enough, a two-story wooden home for his family. Then he added a floor and then another. Sutiagen later said the building simply looked wrong at each stage. unbalanced, unfinished, that adding another level was the only way to make the proportions work. So, he kept going. No architect, no structural engineer, no permits anyone could produce. Just a man, a supply of timber, and a private sense of what the building still needed. By the time he stopped, the tower stood 13 stories tall, roughly 44 m high, built entirely out of wood. It was widely described as one of the tallest wooden houses in the world. The upper floors were rough and unfinished, boards nailed on as they arrived. It leaned. It creaked in the wind. From across the city, it looked like a crooked wooden rocket aimed at the clouds, growing out of a neighborhood of ordinary low buildings. Then all of it came apart in every sense. Sutiagen went back to prison on unrelated charges. While he was gone, the tower stood empty, taking on rain and snow with nobody to maintain it, and it began to rot from the top down. When he came out, the money was gone, and the city had declared the structure an illegal fire hazard, a genuine danger to everything around it. The courts ordered it demolished. In 2008 and 2009, it came down floor by floor, and what remained of the lower section later burned. He spent more than a decade climbing toward the sky in a material that was never going to hold him up there. And the part I cannot get past is not the engineering. It is that he stood at the top of 12 finished floors, looked at what he had made, and thought it needed one more. Now we come to the final three. And this is where Impossible truly earns the word. Number three, the homes that only ghosts could reach. In Mali in West Africa, there is a vast sandstone cliff called the Bandiagara Escarment. It runs for roughly 150 kilometers across the landscape in places rising 500 m straight out of the plane. At its base live the Doon people in villages that have stood for centuries among the most studied cultures in West Africa. But if you lift your eyes high up the cliff face, far above anywhere a person could reasonably climb, you will see something that stops making sense the longer you look at it. Small structures, mud and stone dwellings and graneries built into near vertical rock tucked under overhangs hundreds of meters up. The Doon did not build them. They say so themselves. The people who did are called the Telm, and they were on that cliff before the Doon arrived, going back at least to the 11th century. They built their homes and their burial chambers impossibly high on the escarment in positions that appear to have no route up at all. And they used those chambers to bury their dead. How they got up there has never been settled. The name Telm is usually translated as something close to we found them which is what the Doon called the people who were already there. There are two explanations and both ask you to believe something extraordinary. The Doon tradition is that the Telm could fly or that they had some power to move up the rock that has since gone out of the world. That is what was passed down and it was passed down by people who lived at the base of that cliff and looked at it every day of their lives. The explanation researchers have proposed is climatic. The idea is that the region was significantly wetter centuries ago, that the escarment was covered in dense forest, and that thick vines hanging down the rock gave the telm a natural ladder. As the climate dried, the forest died back, and the way up disappeared with it. So, take your pick. Either an entire people was erased along with the secret of how they lived, or the landscape itself rearranged so completely that it deleted the evidence. I know some of you are going to argue this one does not deserve to be this high, that a cliff dwelling is not as extreme as a house on a rock in a river. Make the case in the comments. I want to read it. From homes hidden high on a cliff to a home that plants itself in the middle of a river and dares the water to come and take it. Number two, the little house that refuses to drown. Near the town of Bajina Bashta in Serbia, the Dina River runs fast and cold. Out in the middle of it, well away from either bank, a bare rock breaks the surface. Sitting on that rock, alone, surrounded on every side by moving water, is a small wooden house. No bridge, no causeway, no road. Just a house on a stone in the current looking for all the world like it floated down the river, got stuck and decided to stay. The story behind it is almost too simple to be satisfying. In 1968, a group of local young men used to swim out to that rock to lie in the sun. The rock was fine for sunbathing and terrible for everything else. So, somebody suggested a shelter. They fied planks and materials out by boat and by hand. Some of it reportedly floated down from up river and they built one. And then the Dina went to work. Over the following decades, the river rose again and again and tore the house off the rock. It took it in the 70s. It took it again later. It took it again after that. By most accounts, the house has been destroyed and rebuilt something like six or seven times. Every single time people went back out to that rock and built it again. Nobody lives there. Nobody is raising a family out there. There is no power and no plumbing. And the house serves no practical purpose whatsoever. It exists for exactly one reason. Because every time the river erased it, human beings looked at that empty stone and decided, "No, the house stays." And that quiet, pointless stubbornness might be the most impossible thing on this entire list. Which brings us to number one. A house you have almost certainly seen already standing completely alone at the edge of the world that has managed to fool most of the internet. Number one, the loneliest house in the world. Off the southern coast of Iceland in the Vest Maner archipelago, a scatter of steep green islands rises out of a cold gray sea. Most of them are empty. Cliffs, grass, seabirds, nothing else. On one of them, there is a single white house. Nothing else at all. No neighbors, no road, no other structure for kilometers of open North Atlantic in every direction. The island is called El. And that one house has become one of the most shared and most argued about images anywhere online because nobody scrolling past it can accept a simple answer. So the internet built better ones. That a reclusive billionaire bought the island and built a bunker there to survive the end of the world. That the singer Bjork was given the island by the Icelandic government. That it is a private retreat for someone very wealthy who wants to disappear. that a hermit lives inside and has not spoken to another human being in decades. One of those has a threat of something real in it. Around the year 2000, there was genuine public discussion in Iceland about offering Bjork the use of an island, and reports at the time did not entirely agree on the details. That conversation is where the myth grew from, and it has been stuck to this photograph ever since. The reality is stranger, mostly because of how ordinary it is. The house was built in the 1950s by a local hunting association as a lodge for men coming to the island to hunt puffins, which has been part of life in these islands for a very long time. There is no electricity. There is no running water, though rainwater is collected. There is a sauna, which surprises people, heated by wood. Nobody lives there permanently. It is on paper a hunting cabin on an empty island. And the myths will not die. Every year the photograph goes viral again. Every year thousands of people see it for the first time and decide immediately and completely that there has to be more to it than a cabin. Maybe that is the real reason it sits at number one. Not because of who lives there. Because of the story every single one of us writes in our own head the second we see it. One small house, no road out, the edge of the map. Every home on this list started in the same place. Somebody stood in a spot that said, "Clearly and obviously, you cannot live here." A frozen plane where the ground will not open. A pillar of stone with no way up. A gap between two buildings less than a meter wide. A rock in a flooding river. An island in an empty sea. And instead of walking away and finding somewhere sensible, they picked up their tools and they stayed. Maybe that is the most human thing we do. Not the walls or the roof or the view out the window. Just the stubborn refusal to accept that anywhere at all is truly impossible to call home. If you made it all the way to the end, I want to hear from you. Which of these would you spend one night in? And which one would you not set foot in for any amount of money in the world? Tell me in the comments and you decide where we go next. Sunken cities swallowed whole by the sea or the deepest places on Earth that nobody has ever reached the bottom of. Say the word, subscribe, and I will see you in the next place the world said could not exist.
fullTextVi: Một ngôi nhà được cho là nơi duy nhất có ý nghĩa trên Trái đất. Bốn bức tường, một mái nhà trên đầu, nền đất vững chắc dưới chân bạn. Đó là điều mà loài người chúng ta đã đồng ý trước khi chúng ta gần như đồng ý bất cứ điều gì khác. Nhưng một số người đã nhìn vào điểm không thể tìm thấy nhất, một vách đá đối mặt với độ cao 200 m, vùng đất hoang băng giá nơi trái đất không bao giờ tan băng, một tảng đá trơ trụi giữa dòng sông lũ và quyết định rằng chính xác là nơi họ muốn sống. Người đàn ông hơn 20 năm một mình trên đỉnh đá cột, dùng dây kéo thức ăn lên không chịu đi xuống. Một thị trấn chìm vào giấc ngủ mỗi đêm bên dưới một phiến đá kích thước của một sân vận động. Cả một cộng đồng đào sâu xuống sa mạc vì bề mặt sẽ giết chết them. Và một ngôi nhà nhỏ màu trắng đứng trơ ​​trọi trên một hòn đảo kỳ lạ đến mức Internet đã phát minh ra một tỷ phú chỉ để giải thích điều đó. Đây là những ngôi nhà điên rồ nhất từng được xây dựng ở những vị trí khó tin nhất trên Trái đất. Trước khi chúng ta bắt đầu, hãy làm điều gì đó cho tôi.
